papers.title: AdaBoN: Adaptive Best-of-N Alignment
papers.core_contribution: A two-stage, prompt-adaptive Best-of-N policy that first estimates each prompt's reward distribution with a small exploration budget and then greedily allocates the remaining samples by estimated marginal value.
papers.methodology: Evaluates adaptive versus uniform inference allocation on AlpacaEval, HH-RLHF, and PKU-SafeRLHF using 12 language-model/reward-model pairs and 50 sampled prompt batches; introduces Batch Win Rate and Expected Survival Time.
papers.key_results: Across 12 LM/RM pairs and 50 prompt batches, adaptive allocation outperforms equal allocation at the same budget and remains competitive with uniform allocation given 20% more budget; some batch win rates reach 70%.
papers.key_results_location: arXiv abstract; ICLR 2026 manuscript, Introduction contributions (items 3-4)
limitations: This is alignment-time reward maximization, not adversarial search against a security target.
Results depend on learned reward models and batch-level prompt distributions; they do not establish live-target transfer or replay-deadline guarantees.
papers.math_foundations: Order statistics for Best-of-N, empirical reward-distribution estimation, marginal value of an additional sample, and greedy resource allocation under a fixed total budget.
papers.motivation: Uniform Best-of-N wastes compute on prompts that are already easy or whose reward tails offer little marginal gain.
constraints_inferred: Inference: use a small mandatory exploration floor per model/guardrail cell before reallocating budget.
Inference: scores must be comparable and stable enough within a cell for estimated marginal gains to be meaningful.
key_decisions: Separate exploration from exploitation.
Allocate by expected marginal portfolio value, not by equal counts or incumbent maximum alone.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Uniform per-prompt allocation is retained as the principal baseline and is empirically dominated at the same budget.
load_bearing_assumptions: Per-prompt reward distributions are sufficiently smooth and stationary over the allocation window.
Applying the same policy to heterogeneous live security cells is an unvalidated analogy; constructed profiles cannot confirm target response heterogeneity.
papers.relevance_reason: The closest direct source for adaptive fixed-budget Best-of-N allocation, but its objective and feedback model are not security attacks.

papers.title: Best-of-N Jailbreaking
papers.core_contribution: Shows that repeated black-box sampling of innocuous input variations yields predictable scaling in attack success and composes effectively with other black-box attacks.
papers.methodology: Samples randomized text, vision, and audio augmentations until a grader identifies a successful response or a maximum N is reached; studies scaling, forecasting, reliability, cross-model difficulty correlations, and attack composition.
papers.key_results: At N=10,000, text ASR is 89% on GPT-4o and 78% on Claude 3.5 Sonnet. At N=100, GPT-4o reaches 50% ASR for a reported $9. Successful variants replay unreliably at temperature 1: mean harmful-response rates are 30% text, 25% vision, and 15% audio. Small-N power-law fits forecast final ASR with mean absolute errors of 4.4, 6.3, and 2.5 percentage points for text, vision, and audio respectively.
papers.key_results_location: paper Sections 3.1, 4.2, and 5.4; arXiv HTML lines 57-60, 100, and 144
limitations: Large N can be expensive and attack success is highly model-, request-, and modality-dependent.
A single discovered success is often not replay reliable.
The fitted power law is empirical and sometimes underpredicts high final ASR.
papers.math_foundations: Best-of-N order statistics; empirical scaling law -log(ASR)=a*N^(-b); bootstrap trajectories; rank correlation of per-request difficulty across models.
papers.motivation: Model stochasticity and sensitivity to benign-looking transformations create an exploitable tail that grows with sampling effort.
constraints_inferred: Inference: candidate selection must score both first-hit success and repeated-trial reliability.
Inference: budget allocation should use per-cell empirical curves, because the N required varies substantially across safeguards.
key_decisions: Maintain multiple independent variants instead of one observed winner.
Reserve repeated evaluations for reliability estimation and compose complementary candidate families when sample-efficient.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Plain resampling without augmentations is much weaker; Appendix D.6 reports unsuccessful attempts to find universal audio augmentations, including poor validation generalization after optimizing a training set.
load_bearing_assumptions: Sampling variations explores a sufficiently rich and stable response distribution.
Observed maxima and arbitrary replay margins are not deadline guarantees; returned-set sizing requires a calibrated tail/dependence model and an explicit void-risk target.
papers.relevance_reason: Direct evidence for black-box Best-of-N scaling, candidate dependence, cross-model heterogeneity, composition, and replay risk.

papers.title: RainbowPlus: Enhancing Adversarial Prompt Generation via Evolutionary Quality-Diversity Search
papers.core_contribution: An adaptive MAP-Elites-style quality-diversity search with multiple candidates per archive cell, diversity filtering, batched probabilistic fitness, and survivor selection.
papers.methodology: Iterates parent sampling, LLM mutation, diversity filtering, response evaluation, and archive update. Compares against quality-diversity baselines on six datasets/four open models and against nine methods on HarmBench across twelve target models; releases code.
papers.key_results: Reports Diverse-Score about 0.84; up to 10,418 unique candidates versus 100 for Rainbow on Ministral-8B-Instruct-2410; mean HarmBench ASR 81.1% versus AutoDAN-Turbo 77.2%; runtime 1.45 versus 13.50 hours.
papers.key_results_location: abstract; Tables 2-4; Discussion, arXiv HTML lines 326-330
limitations: Preprint results rely on an LLM judge and on a reimplementation of the closed-source Rainbow baseline.
High semantic diversity does not by itself imply independence of replay failures or transfer across hidden guardrails.
papers.math_foundations: Evolutionary quality-diversity optimization, MAP-Elites archives, niche-based survivor selection, probabilistic multi-candidate fitness, and explicit behavioral descriptors.
papers.motivation: Single-winner optimization collapses diversity and can miss distinct vulnerability niches; a portfolio should preserve both quality and behavioral coverage.
constraints_inferred: Inference: define archive cells using source-compliant structural features, not sensitive payload strings.
Inference: cap correlated near-duplicates per cell and reserve slots across families/models.
key_decisions: Keep several elites per niche.
Use joint quality and diversity gates before consuming live evaluation budget.
papers.tried_and_discarded: The paper replaces Rainbow's single-prompt-per-cell archive and pairwise fitness comparisons; it notes that Rainbow had to be reimplemented because the original framework was closed source.
load_bearing_assumptions: The behavioral descriptor space captures distinctions that matter to target outcomes.
Judge scores are sufficiently calibrated for selection and are not systematically reward-hacked.
papers.relevance_reason: Provides the clearest portfolio mechanism for jointly preserving effectiveness and diversity under constrained search.

papers.title: Jailbreaking Black Box Large Language Models in Twenty Queries
papers.core_contribution: PAIR uses an attacker model, target feedback, and iterative refinement to search semantic candidates with only black-box access to the target.
papers.methodology: An attacker LLM proposes a candidate, the target responds, an evaluator scores the response, and the attacker uses the transcript and score to refine the next candidate; evaluated across open and closed models.
papers.key_results: PAIR often finds a successful candidate in fewer than 20 target-model queries and reports transfer across GPT-3.5/4, Vicuna, and Gemini; an exact aggregate transfer rate is not reported in the abstract.
limitations: Efficiency counts target queries but not auxiliary attacker/evaluator calls.
Outcomes depend strongly on attacker and evaluator model quality and on target-model versions.
papers.math_foundations: Sequential black-box optimization with an LLM proposal policy, scalar feedback, bounded iterations, and multiple independent streams.
papers.motivation: Gradient access is unavailable for proprietary targets, while semantic feedback can guide a query-efficient search.
constraints_inferred: Inference: preserve independent refinement streams to reduce early local lock-in.
Inference: account separately for target-query cost and auxiliary-model cost.
key_decisions: Use response-conditioned iteration rather than static generation.
Stop a stream on verified success or budget exhaustion.
papers.tried_and_discarded: The paper positions high-query white-box suffix optimization and unguided/static attacks as unsuitable for its black-box, low-query goal; detailed negative trials are not_reported in the abstract.
load_bearing_assumptions: The evaluator score tracks the true target criterion.
Target feedback remains informative across iterations and does not drift during the search.
papers.relevance_reason: Foundational query-efficient feedback loop for adaptive black-box candidate refinement.

papers.title: Tree of Attacks: Jailbreaking Black-Box LLMs Automatically
papers.core_contribution: TAP combines branching search with two-stage pruning: reject off-topic candidates before target queries, then retain only high-scoring survivors for the next depth.
papers.methodology: Uses attacker, evaluator, and target LLMs in a breadth-first tree. At every round it branches candidates, prunes off-topic proposals, queries the target, scores outcomes, and selects a bounded frontier.
papers.key_results: On GPT-4-Turbo, TAP reports 84% success with 22.5 average target queries versus PAIR's 44% with 47.1. Removing off-topic pruning uses 55.4 queries and reaches 72% versus TAP's 22.5 queries and 84%. In the conference paper's transfer table, 34 of 42 candidates found on GPT-4-Turbo transfer to GPT-4o and 31 of 42 transfer to Gemini-Pro.
papers.key_results_location: NeurIPS paper Table 1, page 7; Table 4, page 8; Table 3, page 7
limitations: Reported query efficiency excludes auxiliary attacker/evaluator calls.
Transfer varies sharply by model and is zero in several Llama-2-7B cells.
Evaluator choice can cause severe performance degradation; the authors' audit reports a 13% false-positive rate and 0% false-negative rate for the GPT-4 metric.
papers.math_foundations: Bounded breadth-first tree search, heuristic pruning, beam-like top-k frontier selection, and empirical transfer matrices.
papers.motivation: Branching improves exploration, while pre-target pruning prevents obviously irrelevant candidates from consuming scarce queries.
constraints_inferred: Inference: use a cheap source-compliance and relevance gate before any expensive live call.
Inference: do not treat transfer as global; learn a directional source-to-target matrix with shrinkage for sparse cells.
key_decisions: Branch before committing budget.
Prune twice: first for validity/relevance, then for outcome score.
Carry a small frontier, not just the current best.
papers.tried_and_discarded: A no-off-topic-pruning variant and a branching-factor-one variant are empirically inferior; a weaker evaluator configuration sharply reduces success.
load_bearing_assumptions: The pruning evaluator has high recall for eventual successes.
Auxiliary-model expense and latency are acceptable even though they are omitted from the target-query budget.
papers.relevance_reason: Directly supports query-aware branching, preflight pruning, bounded frontiers, and cell-specific transfer estimates.

papers.title: LASH: Adaptive Semantic Hybridization for Black-Box Jailbreaking of Large Language Models
papers.core_contribution: Treats outputs from heterogeneous attack families as reusable seeds, then searches over seed subsets and softmax mixture weights to synthesize one candidate per target request using only black-box feedback.
papers.methodology: Builds a reduced-budget seed pool from PAIR, TAP, and AutoDAN-Turbo; a composition model combines selected seeds; a derivative-free genetic optimizer updates mixture weights under a two-stage refusal-plus-judge fitness. Evaluation uses 100 JailbreakBench behaviors, six target models, a 160-query cap, and end-to-end query accounting.
papers.key_results: Across six targets, LASH reports 84.50% keyword ASR and 74.50% two-stage ASR with 30.01 mean target queries. The strongest reported baseline averages are 66.83% keyword ASR (FlipAttack) and 40.67% two-stage ASR (TAP). Defended mean two-stage ASR is 41.50% under SmoothLLM, 18.00% under Llama Guard, and 70.83% under perplexity filtering.
limitations: Very recent preprint evaluated on 100 behaviors and six targets with deterministic decoding.
GPT-4o-mini is used as both composer and judge, creating possible correlated model bias.
Per-request attack-family composition is not the same as allocating a global budget across target model/guardrail cells.
papers.math_foundations: Genetic optimization over discrete seed subsets and continuous softmax mixture weights; two-stage fitness; explicit end-to-end query budgeting.
papers.motivation: No single attack family dominates across target models and categories, so complementary candidates should be composed adaptively per request.
constraints_inferred: Inference: enforce small seed-generation budgets so portfolio construction does not hide upstream query costs.
Inference: preserve source-family identity in the ledger to measure which mixtures transfer and which merely overfit the judge.
key_decisions: Seed from multiple structurally distinct search families.
Optimize candidate composition per request rather than selecting a global single best method.
Count both seed generation and adaptive search against the target-query budget.
papers.tried_and_discarded: A seed-oracle that returns the best uncombined seed is outperformed by optimized hybridization on all six targets; uniform weighting is inferior to optimized weights in the reported ablation.
load_bearing_assumptions: The seed families are genuinely complementary and the composer preserves their useful structure.
The two-stage judge is sufficiently aligned with the external success criterion and is not being optimized adversarially.
papers.relevance_reason: The closest direct primary source for black-box, budget-accounted composition of a heterogeneous candidate portfolio.

papers.title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections
papers.core_contribution: Argues that defense evaluation must let the attacker adapt to the defense and scale a common propose-score-select-update loop rather than replay fixed attacks.
papers.methodology: Systematically tunes and scales gradient descent, reinforcement learning, random search, LLM-guided search, and human exploration against each defense's actual mechanism and threat model.
papers.key_results: Bypasses 12 recent defenses spanning four technique families; ASR exceeds 90% for most defenses even though the majority originally reported near-zero ASR. In a human red-teaming study, competitors defeat every challenge considered.
papers.key_results_location: abstract; Figure 1; paper introduction and human red-teaming appendix
limitations: A successful adaptive break falsifies robustness but does not measure typical deployment frequency.
No finite collection of adaptive attacks proves that the strongest possible attacker has been tested.
papers.math_foundations: Stackelberg-style defender-first/adversary-second evaluation; iterative propose-score-select-update optimization under attack-specific budgets.
papers.motivation: Static benchmark strings and weak default attacks systematically overstate defensive robustness.
constraints_inferred: Inference: evaluate each guardrail cell with defense-aware adaptation, while keeping budgets and information access explicit.
Inference: record the full scorer/version/protocol lineage so near-zero local ASR is not mistaken for robust live performance.
key_decisions: Use static tests only as a floor.
Require at least one scaled, defense-adaptive search family per evaluated defense mechanism.
papers.tried_and_discarded: The paper rejects fixed attack corpora and computationally weak untuned optimizers as sufficient evidence for robustness.
load_bearing_assumptions: Adaptive attackers receive the defense knowledge and feedback permitted by the stated threat model.
Reported attacks are strong falsification attempts, not worst-case guarantees.
papers.relevance_reason: Central evidence that allocation and candidate-generation policies must adapt per defense/model cell and that static local evaluations miscalibrate live robustness.

papers.title: AutoDojo: Adaptive Attacks Expose Superficial Defenses and User-Underspecification Limits in LLM Agents
papers.core_contribution: Extends AgentDojo with a cheap black-box loop that iteratively optimizes indirect prompt injections against the deployed defense and separates precisely specified from action-open tasks.
papers.methodology: Runs defense-aware iterative candidate generation and scoring across three task suites, five target models, and prompt-, filter-, and system-level defenses; releases the framework.
papers.key_results: Against a filter with 0% static ASR, AutoDojo recovers 28% ASR overall and 64% on action-open tasks. Adaptive ASR exceeds static ASR against nearly every evaluated defense.
limitations: Very recent preprint evaluated on three suites and five models.
Action-open tasks reveal an underspecified-authority problem that candidate search alone cannot repair.
papers.math_foundations: Iterative black-box optimization with response/rollout feedback; stratified ASR by task authority structure.
papers.motivation: A fixed injection distribution cannot measure whether a defense remains effective after the attack is optimized against it.
constraints_inferred: Inference: stratify evaluation by task authority/underspecification, not only by model and guardrail.
Inference: reserve budget for fresh defense-aware candidates instead of relying entirely on transferred static candidates.
key_decisions: Treat action-open tasks as a distinct high-risk cell.
Report static and adaptive ASR side by side.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Static AgentDojo injections are retained as a baseline but rejected as a sufficient robustness test.
load_bearing_assumptions: The adaptive generator receives enough rollout feedback to optimize against the defense.
Generalizing the measured uplift to live targets requires new evidence; purpose-built response profiles cannot validate live heterogeneity.
papers.relevance_reason: Direct 2026 evidence for defense-aware black-box adaptation in tool-using agents and for adding task authority as an allocation dimension.

papers.title: HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal
papers.core_contribution: A standardized red-teaming evaluation with broad behavior coverage, comparable generation settings, held-out robust graders, and large attack-by-model tables.
papers.methodology: Defines 510 behaviors in four functional categories, fixes the target generation budget, evaluates completions with validated classifiers, and compares 18 red-teaming methods across 33 models/defenses.
papers.key_results: The initial benchmark covers 510 behaviors, 18 methods, and 33 models/defenses. Varying completion length can change substring-metric ASR by up to 30 percentage points, motivating a standardized 512-token generation limit. No evaluated attack or defense is uniformly effective; robustness is uncorrelated with size within six model families spanning 7B-70B parameters.
limitations: Any fixed behavior set, grader, and generation length can itself become a target for overfitting.
The original benchmark emphasizes harmful-content refusal, not the full stateful protocol of a competition or tool-using agent.
papers.math_foundations: Behavior-level attack success rate, validation/test separation, classifier agreement, controlled decoding, and full attack-by-target evaluation matrices.
papers.motivation: Disparate evaluation pipelines and fragile metrics make cross-paper ASR rankings effectively incomparable.
constraints_inferred: Inference: freeze generation limits, grader versions, success criteria, and aggregation before comparing policies.
Inference: report both per-cell results and macro/micro aggregates to expose heterogeneous failure modes.
key_decisions: Use held-out graders and behavior splits.
Standardize every budget-relevant generation parameter.
Retain a complete candidate-by-cell ledger rather than a single headline score.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Substring metrics and evaluation directly on an optimized classifier are rejected as insufficiently robust; nonstandard completion lengths are rejected for cross-method comparisons.
load_bearing_assumptions: The evaluation classifier reflects the intended success definition across nonstandard outputs.
For an executable competition protocol, prose is insufficient unless every state transition, enum, serialization, schema, and ledger update has one computable value.
papers.relevance_reason: Supplies the evaluation discipline needed to diagnose the project's severe local-to-live calibration failures.

papers.title: Security Challenges in AI Agent Deployment: Insights from a Large Scale Public Competition
papers.core_contribution: Turns a large public agent red-teaming competition into the ART benchmark and analyzes query efficiency, transferability, universality, and robustness across heterogeneous deployed-agent scenarios.
papers.methodology: Collects 1.8 million participant submissions against 22 frontier agents in 44 deployment scenarios, curates successful attacks into ART, and reevaluates across 19 models.
papers.key_results: More than 60,000 of 1.8 million submissions produced policy violations. Nearly all agents violate most tested policies within 10-100 queries. The resulting benchmark reaches near-100% ASR across tested agent/policy pairs and shows high cross-model/task transfer, while robustness has limited correlation with model size, capability, or inference-time compute.
limitations: Competition submissions are adaptively selected and the curated benchmark is enriched for successful cases, so prevalence and near-100% ASR are not estimates for random real-world traffic.
Transfer measured on the studied agents and scenarios does not imply stable transfer to unseen model/guardrail cells.
papers.math_foundations: Empirical attack-success distributions, query-to-success curves, cross-model and cross-task transfer matrices, and correlation analyses against capability/size/compute.
papers.motivation: Public competition data offers a high-volume view of which attacks survive heterogeneous agents, tasks, and policies.
constraints_inferred: Inference: seed a portfolio with attacks proven on multiple source cells, but keep exploration budget for target-specific failures.
Inference: calibrate forecasts on held-out time/model/task splits to limit survivor and leaderboard overfitting.
key_decisions: Track query-to-first-success and transfer breadth in addition to ASR.
Separate discovery data from forecast calibration and final evaluation.
load_bearing_assumptions: The curated ART set remains representative enough for comparative stress testing despite survivor selection.
Near-perfect benchmark ASR is a stress-test result, not a calibrated forecast of hidden live-cell performance.
papers.relevance_reason: The closest primary source to a public agent-security competition and direct evidence for query budgets, candidate reuse, and heterogeneous transfer.
